Issued at 1137 PM MDT Sun Sep 20 2026

Fairly quiet through early Tuesday, with just a slight chance of a
few showers and thunderstorms in the Bootheel on Monday, 
spreading a little north and east Monday night. But the pairing of
an early-season back door cold front and a late-season monsoonal
moisture surge will result in some big changes Tuesday through
Thursday.

The first piece of the puzzle will be a backdoor cold front
pushing into the Sacramento Mountains by around midnight Monday
Night/Tuesday morning, and reaching the Rio Grande by dawn. NBM
tried ramping up higher PoPs in the Sacs a little too early. It
looks like fairly shallow moisture will result in fog and low
stratus advecting up to the main ridgeline in the Sacramentos
Monday night into Tuesday morning, with the low clouds shaking 
out some drizzle rather than steady showers or convection. The low
clouds and fog will lift by mid to late morning Tuesday.

Meanwhile, a closed upper low over southern California will weaken
into an open trough by Tuesday morning, while a stalled out
subtropical ridge over Texas blocks its progression. This will
cause the upper level pattern to amplify, with SW flow aloft
backing slightly and pulling up deep subtropical moisture up the
Sierra Madres and into southern New Mexico. That's the second
piece of the puzzle.

The third piece will be a strong subtropical jet over southern
Baja California Monday night, which will help maintain intense
thunderstorms over the Sierra Madres in SW Chihuahua. A
convectively-induced shortwave trough or weak closed upper low
will then roll north, along with the subtropical jet and a broad 
region of upper level diffluence. This shortwave trough (the
fourth piece of the puzzle) will help trigger stronger
thunderstorms Tuesday afternoon. Enhanced mid level flow will
provide 20-30 knots of 0-6km shear, enough for more organized,
longer-lived thunderstorms. The broad upper divergence will
persist through Tuesday night, while a trailing vort lobe
associated with the shortwave trough pivots into south-central New
Mexico. This upper level support will help maintain thunderstorm
development through the night and into Wednesday morning.

The result will be a fairly widespread area of "decent" moderate
rainfall, with the usual smaller pockets of heavy rainfall, aided
by a very moist profile (highly efficient arm rain processes), and
upper level steering flow that favors training. However...as the
event starts coming into range, it appears there is a high
potential that somewhere in this whole mess a more persistent area
of training thunderstorms will develop Tuesday night into
Wednesday morning, with max QPF potential exceeding 3-4 inches in
a 6-12 hour period. 

The backdoor cold front will stall out along the Rio Grande
Tuesday afternoon, with intense moisture convergence developing
along this boundary during the evening hours. The GFS shows a
mid-level jet streak of around 40 knots developing ahead of the 
trailing vort lobe, with a concentrated area of strong theta-e
advection in the 700-500 mb layer. Where this aligns with the
strong low level moisture convergence along the stalled out front,
is likely where the axis of heaviest precip will occur.

Recent model runs, including the 12Z and 18Z ECMWF, 00Z GFS, and
00Z RRFS, and the last few hours of the 00Z HRRR are putting this
focus area right over the Mesilla Valley and El Paso Tuesday night
into Wednesday morning.

However, it is important to point out the the NBM, and the 18Z GFS
and ECMWF ensembles show there is significant spread in where this
area could set up. For example, the NBM mean QPF is fairly useless
at the moment, as it averages out QPF maxes showing up in a wide
range of places. This also becomes apparent when looking at the
NBM QPF max numbers, which place the potential for 3-5 inches 
over wide area.

The "wide area" is anywhere from the Black Range down to Luna 
County, east to the Tularosa Basin and western Hudspeth County.
So, not the entire CWA at least! A Flood Watch has been issued for
this same area, starting Tuesday afternoon (as isolated 
thunderstorms first fire up) into Wednesday evening. The most
critical period looks to be around 3 PM Tuesday through Midday
Wednesday. This could be one of those unusual situations where
heavy rain is ongoing at day break, which could result in impacts
to the morning commute Wednesday. (But again, the narrow band of
heaviest rain could shift into more open desert to the west or 
less-populated areas to the east.) 

After a slug of runoff passed through, the Rio Grande is back to
being empty in the Mesilla and El Paso valleys, which is a bit of
favorable news.  

There is also a "sneaker risk" of isolated severe thunderstorms
Tuesday afternoon, especially in SW New Mexico where both deep- 
layer and low level shear will be maximized.
